title: Chinese Hackberry: The Enoki Trees of Japan's Shrines and Roadsides
meta_description: Japan calls it enoki and once planted it on the milestone mounds of the Tokugawa highways. Nara's Enoki of Wakamiya is five metres round.
intro: In Japan this tree is enoki, and for two and a half centuries it did a job before it did anything ornamental: the Tokugawa shogunate planted one, or a red pine, at every ichirizuka, the paired earthen mounds that marked each ri of the great highways out of Edo, so a traveller had shade to rest in as well as a distance to measure. Shrines took to it for the same reasons: it grows fast, broad and long-lived. The Enoki of Wakamiya in Nara, below Kasuga Taisha, is five metres round and only seventeen tall, put at two to three centuries by the national survey. Kyoto's at the Demizu-guchi gate of the Imperial Palace has a crown ten metres wider than the tree is tall, and a Hiroshima shrine's stands taller than the celebrated wife camphor beside it and has never been given a name.
